title: India: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition

learn.hook: In 2011, about 27 lakh enumerators went door to door to count 121 crore Indians. That huge exercise is the Census.
points: India's population was 1,210.8 million (about 121 crore) in 2011 — about 17.5 per cent of the world's population — on only 2.4 per cent of the world's area. It was second after China in 2011.
A large population is a resource (human resource), but it also puts pressure on limited land, water and other resources.
Population data in India are collected through the Census, conducted every 10 years; the first census was held in 1872 and the first complete census in 1881.
The Census gives data on distribution, density, growth, sex ratio, literacy, workers and other characteristics.

example.q: India has 17.5% of world population on 2.4% of world area. How many times its 'fair share' of people per unit area is that?

learn.reallife: Census data decide how many seats each state gets, where schools and hospitals are built, and how funds are shared under schemes.

learn.hook: Uttar Pradesh alone has more people than Brazil. Rajasthan, India's biggest state, has fewer people than Bihar.
points: India's population distribution is highly uneven.
Uttar Pradesh has the highest population, followed by Maharashtra, Bihar, West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh; together these five have about half of India's population.
Rajasthan, the largest state by area, has only 5.67 per cent of the population.

Population is low in high-altitude areas (Himalayas), arid regions (western Rajasthan), and forested and tribal areas; states like Arunachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand have small shares despite large areas.
On a distribution map, dense dots crowd the northern plains, deltas and coasts; sparse dots appear in the Himalayas, Thar and the north-east hills.

topics.title: Factors influencing population distribution in India

learn.hook: Why are there more people per square km in the Ganga delta than almost anywhere else on Earth? Rivers, soil — and history.
points: Physical factors: terrain, climate and availability of water largely decide distribution. The North Indian plains, deltas and coastal plains have high population; southern and central Indian plateaus, Himalayas and some north-eastern states have lower population.

Socio-economic and historical factors are also important: evolution of settled agriculture and agricultural development, pattern of human settlement, development of transport networks, industrialisation and urbanisation.
Regions with good irrigation and transport (e.g. canal-irrigated plains) attract dense settlement.

Urban regions of Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Bengaluru, Pune, Ahmedabad, Chennai and Jaipur have high concentrations due to industrial development, urbanisation and employment opportunities, attracting rural-urban migrants.

example.q: Why is Pune much more crowded than many parts of the Deccan plateau around it?
steps: Physical factors on the plateau are similar.
But Pune has industries, IT, education and jobs (socio-economic factors).
These attract migrants and raise population.
example.answer: Industrialisation and urbanisation pull people to Pune

learn.reallife: Bengaluru's rapid population growth since the 1990s came from IT jobs — a socio-economic factor, not a physical one.

learn.hook: In 1951, India had 117 people per sq km. By 2011, 382. Every patch of land now carries more than three times as many people.
points: Density of population is the number of persons per unit area. India's density was 382 persons per sq km in 2011, up from 117 in 1951.
Density varies from about 17 persons per sq km in Arunachal Pradesh to over 11,000 in the National Capital Territory of Delhi.

Among states, Bihar has the highest density (over 1,100), with West Bengal next; Uttar Pradesh also has a very high density, and in the Peninsula, Kerala and Tamil Nadu have relatively high densities.

Hilly, dissected and rugged terrain, low rainfall and less fertile soils lead to low density — e.g. most north-eastern states and mountainous states like Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand; Assam has a moderate density.
Map work: mark Bihar, West Bengal and UP as highest-density states, and Arunachal Pradesh as lowest.

example.q: By how many persons per sq km did India's density rise from 1951 to 2011?
steps: Density 2011 = 382.
Density 1951 = 117.

learn.reallife: Bihar's high density puts huge pressure on farmland, which is one reason for large-scale out-migration to other states for work.

learn.hook: Two states have the same population per sq km — but one has mostly rocky hills and the other green fields. Simple density hides the difference.
points: Simple (arithmetic) density = total population ÷ total area; it does not show the pressure on farmland.
Physiological density = total population ÷ net cultivated area.
Agricultural density = total agricultural population ÷ net cultivable area.
Agricultural population includes cultivators and agricultural labourers and their family members.
These measures better show the pressure of population on agricultural land.

example.q: A district has 30 lakh people, of whom 18 lakh are agricultural population, and 6,000 sq km of net cultivated area. Find physiological and agricultural density.
steps: Physiological density = 30,00,000 ÷ 6,000 = 500 persons per sq km.
Agricultural density = 18,00,000 ÷ 6,000 = 300 persons per sq km.
example.answer: Physiological: 500; agricultural: 300 persons per sq km

learn.reallife: Planners use agricultural density to judge where farm holdings are too small and where non-farm jobs are needed most — e.g. in parts of Bihar and eastern UP.

topics.title: Growth of population: meaning and measures

learn.hook: Between 1901 and 2011, India's population grew more than five times — from about 24 crore to 121 crore.
points: Growth of population is the change in the number of people living in a particular area between two points of time; it can be expressed in absolute numbers and as a percentage (growth rate).
Population growth has two components: natural growth (analysed through crude birth and death rates) and induced growth (explained by the volume of inward and outward movement of people).
India's annual growth rate of population was about 1.64 per cent in 2011.
Decadal growth rates (1901–2011) can be read from a table or graph: negative in 1911–21, highest in 1961–71 (24.80%), and falling after 1981 (17.64% in 2001–11).

example.q: India's population was about 102.9 crore in 2001 and 121.1 crore in 2011. Find the growth and the decadal growth rate.

learn.reallife: The 1911–21 decade saw negative growth mainly due to famines and the 1918 influenza epidemic; afterwards India never looked back.

topics.title: Four phases of population growth in India

learn.hook: In 1921, India's population almost stood still. By 1981, it was 'exploding'. What happened in between?
points: Phase I (1901–1921) — stagnant or stationary phase: very low growth (negative in 1911–21); both birth and death rates high; poor health and medical services, illiteracy and inefficient distribution of food and basic necessities.

Phase II (1921–1951) — steady population growth: improvements in health and sanitation reduced mortality; better transport and communication improved distribution; birth rate stayed high — mortality-induced growth.

Phase III (1951–1981) — period of population explosion: rapid fall in mortality with high fertility; average annual growth as high as 2.2%; developmental activities under Five Year Plans improved living conditions; increased international migration from Tibet, Bangladesh, Nepal and Pakistan.

Phase IV (post-1981 to present) — growth rate, though high, started slowing down gradually; the crude birth rate declined due to a rise in the mean age at marriage, improved quality of life and, particularly, education of females.

example.q: Which phase is described by: 'mortality falls fast, fertility stays high, annual growth reaches 2.2%'?
steps: Fast fall in deaths + high births = big gap.
Annual growth of 2.2% is the highest.

learn.reallife: Rising female literacy and later marriages in states like Kerala and Tamil Nadu brought down birth rates first — the Phase IV pattern.

learn.hook: In 1991–2001, Kerala grew by under 10% while Nagaland grew by nearly 65%. Same decade, same country!
points: Population growth rates vary widely among states.
During 1991–2001, the southern states — Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh — along with Odisha, Puducherry and Goa had low growth rates, not exceeding 20 per cent.
Kerala registered the lowest decadal growth rate (about 9.4%) and Nagaland the highest (about 64.5%) during 1991–2001.
A contiguous belt of north-western, northern and north-central states — such as Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Rajasthan, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh — had relatively high growth rates.
During 2001–2011, growth rates declined in most states compared with 1991–2001, a sign that the slowdown is spreading.

learn.hook: One in five Indians is a teenager. That's over 25 crore people between 10 and 19 — India's biggest asset, and its biggest responsibility.
points: Adolescents are people aged 10 to 19 years; they formed about 20.9 per cent of India's population in 2011.
Adolescents are a potential resource for the future, but they are vulnerable if not properly guided.

Challenges: low age at marriage, illiteracy (especially female), school dropouts, low intake of nutrients, high maternal mortality among adolescent mothers, high rates of HIV/AIDS, physical and mental disability, drug abuse and alcoholism, and juvenile delinquency.

The Government has framed the National Youth Policy (latest, 2014) for the holistic development of youth; the National Population Policy also addresses adolescent needs, including education and health.

learn.hook: Seven out of every ten Indians lived in villages in 2011 — in more than 6.4 lakh of them.
points: Population composition covers age, sex, place of residence, ethnic characteristics, tribes, language, religion, marital status, literacy and education, and occupation.

The share of rural population varies among states: Himachal Pradesh and Bihar are very highly rural, while Goa and Maharashtra are relatively urbanised.

learn.hook: Travel 100 km in India and the language often changes. Grierson counted 179 languages and 544 dialects!
points: India is a land of linguistic diversity: according to Grierson's Linguistic Survey of India, there were 179 languages and as many as 544 dialects; the Constitution recognises 22 scheduled languages.

Linguistic families: Austric (Nishada) — Austro-Asiatic: Mon-Khmer (Meghalaya, Nicobar Islands) and Munda (Jharkhand, Odisha, West Bengal etc.); Dravidian (Dravida) — South, Central and North Dravidian; Sino-Tibetan (Kirata) — Tibeto-Myanmari languages of the Himalayas and north-east; Indo-European (Aryan) — Indo-Aryan, the largest family.
Religious composition: Hindus form the majority; Muslims are the largest minority; Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists and Jains are other important groups.

Spatial distribution: Sikhs are concentrated mainly in Punjab, Haryana and Delhi; Christians along the western coast (Goa, Kerala) and in the north-eastern hill states and Chotanagpur; Muslims form a majority in the Kashmir valley and Lakshadweep; most Buddhists live in Maharashtra, and Jains are concentrated in urban areas of Rajasthan, Gujarat and Maharashtra.

topics.title: Working population: main, marginal and non-workers

learn.hook: Only about 4 in 10 Indians worked in 2011. Who are the workers, and what do they do?
points: The Census divides population into main workers (work for at least 183 days, about six months, in a year), marginal workers (work for less than 183 days) and non-workers.
Work participation rate (main + marginal workers as a share of population) was about 39.8 per cent in 2011, leaving about 60 per cent as non-workers — a high dependency ratio.
Work participation tends to be higher in economically less developed states, where many manual workers are needed for subsistence activities.

Census occupational categories: cultivators, agricultural labourers, household industrial workers, and other workers (non-household industries, trade, commerce, construction, repair and other services).
About 54.6 per cent of all workers are cultivators and agricultural labourers; about 3.8 per cent are in household industries and about 41.6 per cent are other workers.

example.q: A villager works on a construction site for 120 days a year and is otherwise unemployed. Is she a main or marginal worker?
steps: Main workers work at least 183 days a year.
120 days < 183 days.
So she is a marginal worker.

learn.reallife: MGNREGA guarantees 100 days of wage work a year to rural households — such work alone would still classify a person as a marginal worker in Census terms.

items.q: Minimum days for a main worker?
Share of cultivators + agricultural labourers in workers (%)?

quiz.q: According to the Census, a main worker works for at least how many days in a year?
quiz.explain: Main workers work at least 183 days (about six months).
steps: Lesson: main workers work at least 183 days (about six months) a year.
So the answer is 183.
Answer: 183

quiz.q: India's work participation rate in 2011 was about:
quiz.explain: About 39.8 per cent of the population were workers.
steps: Lesson: work participation rate in 2011 was about 39.8%.
So the answer is 39.8%.
Answer: 39.8%

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the Census's four occupational categories?
quiz.explain: The fourth category is 'other workers', which includes such jobs; 'software engineers' is not a separate category.
steps: Categories: cultivators, agricultural labourers, household industrial workers, other workers.
'Software engineers' is not a separate category.
So it is the answer.
Answer: Software engineers
quiz.mistake: Thinks every occupation is a category

quiz.q: What share of India's workers are cultivators and agricultural labourers (2011)?
quiz.explain: About 54.6 per cent.
steps: Lesson: about 54.6% of workers are cultivators and agricultural labourers.
41.6% are other workers.
So the answer is 54.6%.
Answer: 54.6%
quiz.mistake: Picks the share of other workers

quiz.q: A person who works for 100 days in a year is classified as a:
quiz.explain: Less than 183 days → marginal.
steps: Rule: less than 183 days a year = marginal worker.
So the person is a marginal worker.
Answer: Marginal worker
quiz.mistake: Thinks any work makes one a main worker

quiz.q: Why is the work participation rate often higher in economically less developed states?
options: Many manual workers are needed for subsistence activities
quiz.explain: Subsistence economies need many hands.
steps: Lesson: less developed states need many manual workers for subsistence activities.
So participation is higher there.
Answer: Many manual workers are needed for subsistence activities

quiz.q: Assertion (A): India has a large proportion of non-workers. Reason (R): Only about 39.8 per cent of the population were workers in 2011.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; R shows that about 60% are non-workers.
steps: Check A: India has many non-workers — true.
Check R: only about 39.8% were workers in 2011 — true.
So about 60% are non-workers; R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Only about 3.8 per cent of workers are in household industries. Reason (R): Household industries employ the largest share of India's workers.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true. R is false — agriculture employs the largest share.
steps: Check A: only about 3.8% of workers are in household industries — true.
Check R: 'household industries employ the largest share' — false.
So A is true, but R is false.
Answer: A is true, but R is false

revise.summary: The Census classes people as main workers (at least 183 days a year), marginal workers (less than 183 days) and non-workers. Work participation was about 39.8% in 2011; about 54.6% of workers are cultivators and agricultural labourers, 3.8% in household industries and 41.6% other workers.

Work participation rate and dependency
The four occupational categories and their shares
remember: Main worker ≥ 183 days a year; marginal < 183 days
Work participation rate 2011 ≈ 39.8%; ~60% non-workers

traps: Household industries do not employ the largest share — agriculture does
100 days of work makes a person marginal, not main

topics.title: Occupational composition: gender and regional patterns

learn.hook: In Nagaland most workers own and till their land; in Andhra Pradesh many work on others' fields; in Delhi most work in services.
points: Male workers outnumber female workers in all three sectors (primary, secondary, tertiary).
The number of female workers is relatively high in the primary sector, though women's participation in secondary and tertiary sectors has been improving.
Himachal Pradesh and Nagaland have a very large share of cultivators.
Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Jharkhand, West Bengal and Madhya Pradesh have a higher proportion of agricultural labourers.

Highly urbanised areas like Delhi, Chandigarh and Puducherry have a very large proportion of workers in 'other services'. Exam focus: census, density types, growth phases, regional variation, adolescents, occupational composition and map work.

example.q: Why does Delhi have a much higher share of 'other workers' than Nagaland?
steps: Delhi is highly urbanised with trade, offices, industry and services.
Nagaland is rural and hilly; most workers are cultivators.
So Delhi's workers are mainly in secondary and tertiary jobs.
example.answer: Urbanisation in Delhi creates service and industrial jobs

learn.reallife: Self-help groups and the rise of women in IT, banking and healthcare are slowly raising female work participation outside agriculture.

quiz.q: Which pair of density measures is used to show pressure on farmland?
quiz.explain: Both relate population to cultivated or cultivable land.
steps: Physiological density uses cultivated area; agricultural density uses cultivable area.
Both relate people to farmland.
So the answer is physiological and agricultural density.
Answer: Physiological and agricultural density
